hints: Focus on the gas test first, a pungent alkaline gas that gives dense white smoke with HCl is a classic signature to recognise.
That gas is only released on warming with NaOH if the solid contains the ammonium ion, so you can narrow T down to two possibilities.
Consider the barium chloride result, think about which white precipitate survives in dilute HCl and which one would dissolve with fizzing.
walkthrough:
**Identify the cation from the gas test**

Great start, let's decode that pungent gas. It turns damp red litmus blue, so it is alkaline, and it forms dense white smoke of ammonium chloride with HCl gas. That is ammonia, $\text{NH}_3$.

Chemical test:
$$\text{NH}_3(g) + \text{HCl}(g) \rightarrow \text{NH}_4\text{Cl}(s) \text{ white smoke}$$

**Link ammonia to ammonium in T**

Ammonia is not in the solid to start with. It is made when an ammonium salt is warmed with sodium hydroxide.

Governing reaction:
$$\text{NH}_4^+ + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
So T must contain $\text{NH}_4^+$. That leaves only ammonium carbonate or ammonium sulfate.

**Identify the anion with barium chloride**

Now use the second test. Barium chloride gives a white precipitate with both carbonate and sulfate, but their behaviour in acid is different.

Reactions to compare:
$$\text{Ba}^{2+} + \text{SO}_4^{2-} \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4(s) \text{ white, insoluble in dilute HCl}$$
$$\text{Ba}^{2+} + \text{CO}_3^{2-} \rightarrow \text{BaCO}_3(s) \text{ white, dissolves in dilute HCl with fizzing}$$
Since the precipitate did NOT dissolve in dilute HCl, the anion must be sulfate. Ammonium plus sulfate gives ammonium sulfate.

options.A: Ammonium carbonate would pass the first test because it contains $\text{NH}_4^+$ and would release $\text{NH}_3$ with NaOH. However it fails the second test because $\text{BaCO}_3$ is a white precipitate that dissolves in dilute HCl with effervescence of $\text{CO}_2$, it does not remain insoluble.
options.B: Ammonium sulfate fits both clues perfectly. The $\text{NH}_4^+$ gives $\text{NH}_3$ on warming with NaOH, and the $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ gives white $\text{BaSO}_4$ with barium chloride which is insoluble in dilute HCl.
options.C: Sodium carbonate contains no ammonium, so warming with NaOH would give no ammonia gas, no blue litmus change and no white smoke with HCl. It also gives $\text{BaCO}_3$ which would dissolve in dilute HCl, opposite to the observation.
options.D: Sodium sulfate would correctly give insoluble white $\text{BaSO}_4$ with barium chloride, but it contains $\text{Na}^+$ not $\text{NH}_4^+$. Warming with NaOH would produce no gas, so the first observation rules it out.
